Independent hobby project · SMS-based submersible-pump system

GSM pump control,
monitoring & protection.

During COVID, I took this hobby project from idea to field operation entirely independently: I conceptualised, planned, designed, built, programmed, tested, and integrated the system myself.

Field-tested in 2020–21Text commands · No internet requiredCustom electronics & firmware
3–4 field prototypesEvaluated over months of operation with existing agricultural motor starters.
Control + monitoring + failure prevention

Controller capabilities

  • Monitor: motor load/current, supply voltage and phase availability, running status, and operating schedule.
  • Check continuously: phase readiness and valid two-phase or three-phase supply conditions.
  • Protect: detect dry-run, underload, and overload conditions; stop the motor and send an SMS alert when configured limits are breached.
  • Coordinate: work with capacitor-assisted phase converters and existing two-phase or three-phase starter hardware.
  • Schedule: accept operating schedules, set timers, and shut down after the programmed duration.
  • Control by text: start/stop commands, status notifications, automatic/manual modes, and settings retained across power interruptions.
Field testingHardware developmentEarly circuit testingProject outcome
2020–21 · From a local problem to field operation

A practical response to risks I saw firsthand.

In the Krishna River basin, I saw farmers struggle to operate the pumps supplying their irrigation pipelines. Some installations had no road access. Rain and bad weather made the journey harder, while unpredictable electricity meant repeated trips, sometimes at night. Farmers faced the fear of wild animals and the risk of electrocution around wet, high-power electrical equipment. Operating a pump could demand far more effort and risk than it should.

I could not find a commercially available controller tailored to this combination of local conditions and existing starter hardware. During COVID, I decided to build one myself. Before ChatGPT was available, I drew on my physics background and interest in electronics to work through the sensing, control, communication, and power-supply challenges. I independently developed the circuits and firmware, tested the interfaces, and kept refining the design as real installations exposed problems that did not appear on the workbench.

By 2020–21, I had taken the idea into working field prototypes. Farmers could use ordinary text messages to operate their pumps and receive status information, with electrical monitoring, scheduling, and protective shutdown built into the system. It was a hobby project with a purpose close to home: reducing the need for difficult trips to the river and giving farmers more control over equipment they depended on.

What I tested and resolved

  • Real installations: approximately three to four prototypes, including systems with roughly 10 HP centrifugal pumps.
  • Starter compatibility: phase checks, start-ready signals, and timing coordinated with existing motor-control hardware.
  • Electrical disturbances: traced controller resets near contactors and voltage drops during GSM transmission.
  • Improved stability: refined regulation, filtering, decoupling, local energy storage, and transient suppression.
Hardware development

From interconnected modules to a custom PCB.

I developed the electronics and embedded C/C++ firmware together, then redesigned the modular system into a compact board to simplify wiring, assembly, and integration.

Phase 1 · Module-based prototype

Integrate, program, and field-test.

  • Arduino Uno R3 / ATmega328P: automation and motor-control logic.
  • SIM800L GSM/GPRS: SMS commands, status updates, and notifications.
  • ACS712 30A + current transformer: motor-current sensing and abnormal-load detection.
  • 5V dual-channel relay module: interface to existing starters and contactors.
  • AC-DC / DC-DC modules: low-voltage power conversion and regulation.
  • External phase/voltage interface: supply availability and operating-condition monitoring.
Phase 2 · Custom PCB

Redesign and integrate the circuitry.

  • ATmega328P + SIM800L interface: onboard control and GSM connectivity without a separate Arduino board.
  • MB10S rectifiers + H11L1 optocouplers: optically isolated AC phase detection, replacing separate transformer-based sensing modules.
  • 74HC14 Schmitt triggers: stable digital phase-status signals.
  • Four Songle 5V relays: integrated starter-control switching channels.
  • Hi-Link HLK-20M05: isolated 5V, 20W AC-DC power supply.
  • Current-sensor interfaces + protection: external sensing connections, MOV surge suppression, filtering, and decoupling.

A complete development cycle, owned end to end.

I prepared the schematic and PCB layout, ordered and assembled the boards, and tested programming, communication, and relay operation.

  • Less wiring: integrated circuitry replaced multiple interconnected modules.
  • More compact assembly: fewer separate boards and simpler external connections reduced assembly effort and component cost.
  • Board-level troubleshooting: investigated relay flicker with the initial onboard supply by tracing voltage levels, return paths, and transient loading.

The modular prototypes were field-tested. The custom PCB demonstrated the integrated architecture and core functions; board testing identified further power-supply revisions for the next version.

Early circuit testing

Developing each interface on the workbench.

Breadboard testing let me check the microcontroller, GSM communication, current sensing, and relay interfaces separately before integrating them. Accessible wiring made it easier to isolate faults and verify supply levels as I developed the firmware.

Project outcome

Independent engineering with a practical purpose.

I took a farming-community problem through circuit design, firmware, field operation, troubleshooting, and a custom PCB redesign. The result was a field-tested approach to remote pump operation, electrical monitoring, scheduling, and protective shutdown, built to work with existing irrigation infrastructure.
